deep.reconstruction:
Folio 26r is a draft cover letter, not a working page. It accompanies the 1859 Berlin Academy paper 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse'. The recipient is addressed only as 'Hochverehrtester Herr Professor'. My guess is J. F. Encke, secretary of the Academy's physical-mathematical class and recipient of Gauss's 1849 prime-frequency letter and table; this is uncertain. Weierstrass is the addressee of the different draft on the next page.

Contents of the letter:
(a) Riemann thanks the addressee for lending Gauss's table on the frequency of primes. He returns it, having made a copy that he proposes to file as a commentary to the prime table in Gauss's Nachlass in Göttingen.
(b) He encloses a compressed account of his own research for presentation to the Academy. If it is too long for the Monatsberichte, he asks that at least the results be printed.
(c) He thanks the Academy for his election as corresponding member (August 1859), which dates the draft to autumn 1859.

The summary of results, in modern notation:

1. F(x) = pi(x) for x not prime, and pi(x) - 1/2 at a prime p (the normalized prime-counting function; 'um 1/2 größer' means one half more than the count of primes below p).

2. f(x) = sum_{n>=1} (1/n) F(x^{1/n}). This is Riemann's Π(x), also written J(x) = sum over prime powers p^k <= x of 1/k.

3. psi(x) = sum_{n>=1} exp(-n^2 pi x), the theta-type series.

4. xi(t) = 4 ∫_1^∞ d[x^{3/2} psi'(x)]/dx · x^{-1/4} cos((t/2) log x) dx. This is exactly the integral representation in the published paper. In modern terms xi(t) = Ξ(t) = ξ(1/2 + i t), with ξ(s) = (1/2) s(s-1) π^{-s/2} Γ(s/2) ζ(s).

5. alpha denotes the roots of xi(alpha) = 0. These are 'probably all real', which is the Riemann Hypothesis stated in the t-variable. In any case |Im alpha| < 1/2, i.e. the zeros lie in the critical strip.

6. The explicit formula:
 f(x) = Li(x) - Σ_α [Li(x^{1/2+αi}) + Li(x^{1/2-αi})] + ∫_x^∞ dt / ((t^2-1) t log t) + log xi(0).
 The sum runs over the roots with positive real part, taken in order of size.

7. Möbius inversion:
 F(x) = Σ_m (-1)^μ (1/m) f(x^{1/m}).
 Here m runs over squarefree integers (the 'außer 1' insertion) and μ is the number of prime factors of m, so the coefficient is the Möbius function μ(m).

Riemann then states his wish that 'practical calculators' learn of the formula. He hopes one of them will undertake an actual count of primes and compare it with the law in his formula. In that case he would compute the constants himself: log xi(0) and the smallest roots of xi(alpha) = 0. He would also supply a copy of the Gauss table.

The opening lines at the top of the page are an earlier draft of this same paragraph, later rewritten at the bottom.

No derivation is carried out on the page; everything is stated without proof.
errors: The constant log xi(0) is the same slip as in the printed 1859 paper (noted by Edwards). With Riemann's xi(t) = ξ(1/2 + i t), xi(0) = ξ(1/2) ≈ 0.4971. The correct constant in J(x) = Li(x) - Σ_ρ Li(x^ρ) - log 2 + ∫_x^∞ ... is -log 2 = log ξ(s=0), with ξ(0) = 1/2. So log xi(0) ≈ -0.6989 versus the correct -0.6931.

Historically interesting: Riemann offers to 'compute the numerical value of log xi(0)'. This suggests the slip was genuine, since he treats the constant as one needing computation rather than recognising it as -log 2 (i.e. ξ evaluated at s = 0 or 1).
Ordering the zero sum 'by size' and the convergence of the explicit formula are asserted without proof. Rigorous proofs came with von Mangoldt (1895).
'Probably all real' is the Riemann Hypothesis, an unproved conjecture. The strip bound |Im α| < 1/2 (rather than ≤) was itself only proved later, by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin in 1896.
Li(x^ρ) for complex ρ needs a branch convention, which Riemann discusses in the paper but not here. This is not an error in the letter.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is exactly the published 1859 summary, including the known log xi(0) slip. Two biographical details are mildly notable: the explicit offer to compute the lowest zeros of xi for a 'practical calculator', and the handling of Gauss's prime table. Both fit what Siegel later revealed about Riemann's computations of the lowest zeros. Draft letters of this kind in the Nachlass have probably been described by historians, but I am unsure of the details.

checkable.asserts: ξ(s=0) = 1/2, so the correct constant is log(1/2) = -log 2
The integral formula for xi(t) at t=0 gives ≈ 0.4971 = ξ(1/2), consistent with xi(t) = ξ(1/2 + i t)
The smallest positive real root alpha of xi(alpha)=0 is ≈ 14.1347 (value ≈ 0)
The correction integral at x=2 is ≈ 0.14, finite and positive

transcription_corrections: First (draft) line: 'kräftiger Freund' is probably 'tüchtiger Freund', as in the rewritten paragraph lower down.
'den ich mit größtem Interesse gelesen habe' should likely read 'die ich ...', referring to the Tafel (feminine).
The interlinear '{+zu legen+}' after 'beizufügen' is doubtful; the insertion above the line appears to belong to 'gütigst ... vorzulegen' / 'der Akademie'.
Signature reads 'B. Riemann'; the image shows something like 'L. Riemann', but 'B.' is clearly intended.
'durch kein Quadrat {+außer 1+}': the inserted word is 'außer 1', placed above 'Quadrat', as transcribed.

The opening four lines are a struck-through and partially rewritten earlier version of the later paragraph 'Es ist mir daran gelegen ...'. Its start reads 'Es ist mir daran gelegen' over a deleted word.
